analysis.one_liner: Caps wholesale prices of brand-name prescription drugs by conditioning tax deductions and credits on price agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with a single Democratic cosponsor, referred to two House committees, and never received a hearing or vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate four-year agreements with makers of brand-name prescription drugs (those still under patent or market exclusivity) setting a maximum wholesale price, taking both affordability and the need to fund research into account. To pressure companies into signing, it would deny the federal tax deduction for advertising and marketing a brand-name drug, and the foreign tax credit on its income, unless a pricing agreement was in effect for the whole year. It also created a five-member advisory panel to recommend prices for 50 important or most-prescribed drugs, and let the Secretary inspect manufacturers' financial records and impose negotiated penalties for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and families who pay for brand-name prescription drugs, since negotiated maximum wholesale prices would directly cap what manufacturers can charge; insurers, employers, and government programs that buy those drugs would also pay less.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the HHS Secretary to negotiate agreements with brand-name drug manufacturers establishing a maximum wholesale price, taking into account the drug's affordability relative to the public-health need for it.

Denies the federal deduction for advertising, promoting, or marketing a brand-name drug, and the foreign tax credit on income from manufacturing it, unless a qualified pricing agreement is in effect for the entire taxable year — the leverage meant to bring manufacturers to the table.

Establishes a five-member Advisory Panel on Drug-Price Negotiations, including consumer, minority-consumer, academic, and industry representatives, to recommend prices for the 25 drugs most important to public health and the 25 most commonly prescribed drugs.

Requires price monitoring, allows the Secretary access to manufacturers' financial records, and requires each agreement to specify a liquidated penalty large enough to deter violations, with loss of tax benefits if the manufacturer does not comply.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would accept lower wholesale prices on their monopoly-period drugs or forfeit valuable advertising tax deductions and foreign tax credits; to the extent lower prices trimmed research budgets, some future drug development could be slower.

drawbacks.text: The price cap is not a direct mandate: a manufacturer that refuses an agreement loses only the advertising/marketing deduction and the foreign tax credit for that drug, so the whole scheme depends on tax-code pressure rather than enforceable price control.

The bill itself requires that pricing agreements account for the manufacturer's need to invest in research and development, an acknowledgment that lower monopoly-period prices could mean less spending on developing new drugs.

Enforcement rests on penalties negotiated into each agreement and on the Secretary's monitoring; if a penalty proves too small to deter violations, the main consequence for a noncompliant manufacturer is simply losing the tax benefits for that drug.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing high prices on brand-name drugs still under patent, the benefits are direct and large: a negotiated ceiling on wholesale prices for every brand-name drug whose maker wants to keep tax benefits. The costs fall almost entirely on drug manufacturers, though an honest supporter would concede the indirect mechanism leaves gaps (a company can simply absorb the lost tax benefits) and that squeezing monopoly-period prices could modestly slow new drug development. On balance the bill trades a narrow set of corporate tax advantages for broad price relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to a health subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown introduced the Sustainable Drug Pricing Act in the House on July 22, 2004.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee, because it touched both health policy and the tax code.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken.
The bill ended the Congress with a single Democratic cosponsor and no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote before the 108th Congress expired on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: they kept both their pricing freedom and their advertising tax deductions and foreign tax credits, because the bill never advanced far enough to threaten either.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its sole cosponsor were both Democrats, and the bill died in committees controlled by Republicans without any recorded votes on the merits; no roll calls exist on this bill.

industries.note: Companies selling drugs still under patent or market exclusivity would have to accept a negotiated maximum wholesale price — or give up the advertising/marketing tax deduction and the foreign tax credit for that drug. Their interest in keeping monopoly-period prices free of caps runs against patients' interest in paying less.

Denying the tax deduction for advertising brand-name drugs would reduce spending on pharmaceutical ads, which flow to media outlets and ad agencies. The loss is secondary to the bill's main effect on drug pricing.

The bill's pricing agreements apply only to brand-name drugs with market exclusivity, so generics are untouched while their brand-name competitors face price ceilings — a relative advantage in the market.
